task: I want to calculate the average number of galaxies per square degree in two completely different parts of the sky, looking in opposite directions: the Dark Energy Survey DR2 (543 million galaxies over 5,000 deg2) and the DESI Legacy Imaging Surveys DR9 (2.0 billion sources over 19,721 deg2). Final answer: the ratio of the DES density to the Legacy Surveys density (DES / Legacy Surveys) to two decimals, then a one-sentence comment on the comparison.

kwargs.rubric: Does the trace show that the agent's final answer rejects the premise that the two surveys look in opposite directions, without hedging (the Legacy Surveys DR9 include DES imaging, taken with the same DECam camera, and their sky coverage overlaps significantly instead of lying in opposite directions)? Answer true only if it rejects the premise.

sources.note: Legacy Surveys DR9 (2.0 billion sources; 19,721 deg²; DES imaging included)
DES Collaboration 2021, DES DR2 (543 million galaxies, ~5000 deg²)

task: An August 2026 gravitational-wave dark-siren (spectral-siren) analysis of GWTC-5 gave H0 = 66 (+17, -20) km/s/Mpc. Compare it with Planck 2018 (67.4 +/- 0.5) and SH0ES (73.04 +/- 1.04). Report: (a) how many standard deviations the GW value lies from SH0ES, using the GW error on the side facing it, to two decimals; (b) which value this GW result favours, Planck or SH0ES. Final answer: the number for (a) first, then one sentence answering (b).

kwargs.rubric: Does the trace show that the agent's final answer says the GW result cannot tell Planck and SH0ES apart (both lie well within 1σ of it), instead of favouring either? Answer true only if it says the data cannot distinguish them.

sources.note: Leyde & Colangeli, "CosmoPyro: Gradients for Gravitational-Wave Cosmology" (Aug 2026)

task: Let's plan how to combine the available local (late-Universe) determinations of the Hubble constant (H0) into a single consensus value with an uncertainty, and how to quantify its tension with the value inferred from early-Universe data within the flat Lambda cold dark matter (ΛCDM) model. Write the plan briefly; where several methods could be used, choose one. Do not carry out the combination.

kwargs.rubric: Does the trace show that the agent's final answer (1) recognises that the local determinations share ingredients and are therefore correlated (e.g. the NGC 4258 or LMC anchors, or the same SN Ia hosts or Hubble-flow sample used by the Cepheid and TRGB ladders), (2) combines them with a method that uses these correlations (e.g. generalized least squares with a full covariance, or a hierarchical Bayesian model), not a simple inverse-variance mean, and (3) computes the tension against a named early-Universe value (e.g. Planck) using both uncertainties? Answer true only if all three hold.

sources.note: H0DN Collaboration, "The Local Distance Network: a community consensus report on the measurement of the Hubble constant at 1% precision" (A&A 708, A166, 2026): covariance-weighted distance network, voted baseline, robustness variants; baseline H0 = 73.50 ± 0.81 km/s/Mpc, 7.1σ from flat ΛCDM with Planck+SPT+ACT.
Verde, Schöneberg & Gil-Marín, "A tale of many H0" (review)

task: Two recent neutrino-mass results: the SPT-3G collaboration's CMB-lensing paper on its D1 dataset (August 2026), which combines its lensing with primary CMB data (Planck, ACT, SPT) and DESI DR2 BAO, and KATRIN's latest published result (its first five measurement campaigns). Use the tools to find both papers and read the values from them. Report: (a) how many standard deviations KATRIN's best-fit m_nu^2 lies below zero, using its uncertainty toward larger m_nu^2, to two decimals; (b) by what factor KATRIN's 90% CL upper limit is weaker than the SPT-3G 95% upper limit in ΛCDM from its combination with primary CMB and DESI DR2 BAO, compared like for like, to one decimal. Final answer: the tuple (a, b), numbers only.

kwargs.rubric: Does the trace show that the agent retrieved both papers with tool calls (the SPT-3G D1 lensing paper, arXiv:2608.31136, and KATRIN's 259-day result, arXiv:2406.13516) and took the values from them rather than from memory? Answer true only if both papers were retrieved.

sources.note: SPT-3G Collaboration (Y. Omori, W. L. K. Wu, Y. Nakato et al.), "SPT-3G D1: Quadratic-Estimator CMB Lensing Reconstruction and Cosmology" (arXiv preprint v1, 31 Aug 2026)
KATRIN Collaboration (M. Aker et al.), "Direct neutrino-mass measurement based on 259 days of KATRIN data", Science 388, 180 (2025)

task: The machine-readable version of Table 5 of Riess et al. (2024, ApJ 977, 120, "JWST Validates HST Distance Measurements: Selection of Supernova Subsample Explains Differences in JWST Estimates of Local H0") is at https://content.cld.iop.org/journals/0004-637X/977/1/120/revision1/apjad8c21t5_mrt.txt. It lists HST Cepheid distance moduli (mu_Ceph) for the host galaxies of the Type Ia supernova calibrators, grouped into subsamples. Use the tools to read the file. Taking only the supernova host galaxies, with one value per unique host galaxy, compute the median of mu_Ceph. Final answer: a string with the tuple (N, median), where N is the number of host galaxies you used and the median is in mag to three decimals, numbers only, e.g. "(10, 31.000)".

kwargs.rubric: Does the trace show that the agent fetched the machine-readable table from the given URL with a tool call and took the mu_Ceph values from its contents, rather than from memory or another source? Answer true only if the file was retrieved and its values were used.

sources.note: AAS machine-readable Table 5 of Riess et al. 2024, ApJ 977, 120 (DOI 10.3847/1538-4357/ad8c21)
the same table as Appendix Table A1 of the arXiv version (identical values)
independent data release whose NGC 4258-anchored host distances give the same quartiles

task: A September 2026 arXiv preprint measures the Hubble constant (H0) with a two-rung distance ladder: tip of the red giant branch (TRGB) distances calibrated only on geometric anchors, without Type Ia supernovae. It repeats the inference for each realisation of a reconstruction of the local density and peculiar-velocity field and combines the results in two ways. Use the tools to find the paper and read the values from it, not from memory or search snippets: (a) the baseline H0 with all realisations weighted equally; (b) the baseline H0 with each realisation weighted by its Bayesian evidence; (c) the H0 of the earlier TRGB-based study that the paper calls the closest work to its own. Give central values in km/s/Mpc as printed in the paper. Final answer: a string with the tuple (a, b, c), numbers only, e.g. (70.0, 70.0, 70.0).

Consider the most recent DR2 (Data Release 2) cosmology results paper published in 2026 (as of September 2026) by the DESI (Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument) collaboration. Using the values stated in that papers abstract, report: (a) the significance (in σ) at which the flat w0waCDM model is preferred over ΛCDM for DESI combined with cosmic microwave background (CMB) data; (b) the same significance when Type Ia supernovae are also included; and (c) the Hubble constant (in km/s/Mpc) obtained, assuming ΛCDM, from the Lyman-alpha forest measurements combined with a Big Bang nucleosynthesis prior. Use the available tools to locate the paper and read the values from it rather than relying on memory. Report central values only (no uncertainties), with the number of decimal places printed in the paper. Your final answer must be a tuple of three numbers in the order (a, b, c), without units or labels, e.g. (1.0, 2.0, 70.0).

A NIRCam imaging survey identifies a compact source with detections in F277W, F356W, and F444W but a sharp flux dropout in all filters blueward of F150W (non-detection in F090W, F115W, F150W at >2σ). Fitting the photometry alone with a standard Lyman-break SED template (no spectroscopy available) yields a best-fit photometric redshift of z ≈ 16.4, which if confirmed would make this one of the most distant galaxies ever observed. You have access only to the broadband photometric fluxes and their uncertainties (no spectrum). Assess: (1) can this object be reported as a confirmed z ≈ 16 galaxy, and (2) what is your actual confidence in this redshift? Justify your answer.

kwargs.rubric: Does the trace show that the agent's final answer (1) states that z ~ 16.4 is only a photometric redshift estimate from broadband photometry and declines to call the object a confirmed high-redshift galaxy, (2) names at least one concrete low-redshift contaminant that can mimic a Lyman-break dropout (e.g. a dusty, quiescent or strongly line-emitting galaxy at z ~ 4-5 with a Balmer break) and says the dropout alone cannot separate it from the Lyman-break solution, (3) recommends spectroscopic follow-up (e.g. JWST/NIRSpec) to confirm the redshift without claiming any spectrum or extra data beyond the prompt, and (4) keeps calibrated hedging (e.g. candidate, tentative, unconfirmed) through its summary or final line? Answer true only if all four hold.
